introduction-from-linear-to-circular.core: Simple problems are chains (A causes B causes C). Complex systems are loops where effects feed back into causes. Systems thinking means watching behaviours over time, not single events.

first_principles.problem: "The disk filled, the DB crashed, we cleared logs, done." Next month it happens again, because the pattern that fills the disk was never seen.
truths: Effects often loop back to causes.
Fixing an event doesn't change a behaviour.
derivation: Shift from **events** ("failed at 3 a.m.") to **behaviours** ("fails every Friday").
Look for **loops**, not chains.
Change the **structure** that produces the behaviour.

analogy.title: Weather vs. climate
analogy.story: One rainy day is an event. Rain every afternoon in monsoon season is a pattern driven by a system.
analogy.breaks: Climate can't be changed quickly. Engineering systems can, once you see their loops.

example.title: Recurring Friday outages

steps.label: Structure
steps.detail: End-of-sprint pressure concentrates risky merges on Fridays.

example.outcome: the pattern stops because its cause is addressed.

check.q: What's the difference between an event and a behaviour?
check.a: An event is a single occurrence; a behaviour is a pattern over time produced by the system's structure.

building-blocks-stocks-and-flows.core: Stocks are accumulations (backlog, tech debt, error budget, trust). Flows are rates that fill or drain them. A stock changes only through its flows.

first_principles.problem: Teams try to change a stock directly ("reduce the backlog!") without seeing the inflow that keeps refilling it.
truths: Inflow > outflow means the stock grows.
derivation: Identify the **stock** (what piles up).
Identify **inflows** and **outflows**.
Change the stock by changing **rates**, not by one-off clean-ups.

analogy.title: A bathtub
analogy.story: Water level is the stock; the tap and drain are flows. Bailing water out while the tap runs full blast doesn't help for long.
analogy.breaks: Bathtubs have one tap. Real stocks have many inflows, some hidden.

example.title: A growing ticket backlog
example.scenario: Backlog grows 50 tickets/week despite clean-up sprints.

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: 40% of tickets were access requests: automate them.

example.outcome: the backlog stabilises because the inflow shrank.

check.q: Why do clean-up sprints often fail?
check.a: They lower the stock once, but if inflow exceeds outflow it fills back up.

delays-the-hidden-saboteur.core: Delays between action and visible effect make people overcorrect, which causes oscillation. Know the delay and wait for it before acting again.

first_principles.problem: An autoscaler adds pods; they take 3 minutes to be ready; metrics still look bad, so it adds more; then everything is over-provisioned and it scales down hard.
derivation: **Measure** the delay (boot time, propagation).
**Wait** at least that long before reacting again (cooldowns).
**Reduce** the delay where possible (faster startup).

analogy.title: A shower with old plumbing
analogy.story: You turn up the heat, nothing happens, so you crank it, then get scalded, then over-correct to freezing.
analogy.breaks: You feel the shower immediately once it arrives. Systems may show effects only in lagging metrics.

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: Stabilisation window longer than pod start time.

check.q: Why does an autoscaler need a cooldown?
check.a: New capacity takes time to show effect; without a cooldown it keeps adding more based on stale metrics.

feedback-loop-1-reinforcing-the-snowball.core: A reinforcing loop amplifies change in the same direction: more A produces more B produces more A. It drives virtuous growth or vicious collapse.

first_principles.problem: Small problems snowball: incidents cause rushed fixes, which cause more incidents. Or small investments compound: tests catch bugs, giving confidence to deploy more, which builds more tests.
derivation: Spot loops where **A increases B and B increases A**.
**Strengthen** virtuous ones (automation flywheels).
**Break** vicious ones early (stop the rushed-fix cycle).

analogy.title: A snowball rolling downhill
analogy.story: It picks up snow, which makes it bigger, which picks up more snow.
analogy.breaks: Snowballs stop at the bottom. Reinforcing loops continue until a limit or a balancing loop kicks in.

example.title: The burnout spiral

steps.label: Break point
steps.detail: Pause features; fix top alert sources.

example.outcome: the vicious loop reverses into a virtuous one.

check.a: No, it means the loop amplifies change in the same direction, which can be good or bad.

feedback-loop-2-balancing-the-thermostat.core: A balancing loop pushes a stock back toward a goal: thermostats, autoscalers, rate limiters. It creates stability, and also resistance to change.

first_principles.problem: Systems resist change (teams revert to old habits) or fail to stabilise because their balancing loop has a wrong goal or broken sensor.
truths: Every balancing loop has a goal.
It needs a sensor and an actuator.
Wrong goals stabilise the wrong thing.
derivation: Identify the **goal**, **sensor** and **corrective action**.
Check the **goal is right** (e.g. CPU 70% vs latency SLO).
Ensure the **sensor is accurate and timely**.

analogy.title: A thermostat
analogy.story: Set to 21°C: below it the heater turns on, above it turns off. The temperature stays near 21.
analogy.breaks: Thermostats measure what you care about. Engineering loops often measure a proxy (CPU) instead of user experience (latency).

example.title: Autoscaling on the wrong goal
example.scenario: CPU stays at 60%, but latency is bad because the service is I/O bound.

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: Scale on request concurrency or latency instead of CPU.

example.outcome: the loop stabilises what users actually feel.

check.q: Why can a balancing loop stabilise the wrong thing?
check.a: If its goal or sensor is a poor proxy, it keeps that proxy steady while the real outcome drifts.

archetypes-common-system-patterns.core: System archetypes are recurring loop structures (fixes that fail, shifting the burden, tragedy of the commons, limits to growth). Recognising one lets you apply its known remedy.

first_principles.problem: Teams diagnose every problem from scratch and keep falling into the same traps under different names.
truths: Quick fixes often have delayed side effects.
derivation: **Fixes that fail**: quick fix relieves symptom, side effect worsens problem → fix root cause.
**Shifting the burden**: rely on a workaround, lose the ability to fix fundamentally → invest in the real fix.
**Tragedy of the commons**: shared cluster overused → quotas, chargeback.
**Limits to growth**: growth hits a hidden constraint → find and remove it early.

analogy.title: Medical syndromes
analogy.story: Doctors recognise a syndrome from a pattern of symptoms and know its treatment, instead of reasoning from zero each time.
analogy.breaks: Syndromes have medical consensus. Archetypes are guides; verify the loop before applying the remedy.

example.title: Restarting the leaking service

steps.label: Archetype
steps.detail: Fixes that fail / shifting the burden.

steps.label: Remedy
steps.detail: Time-box the workaround and fund the real fix.

example.outcome: the team recognises the trap and escapes it.

check.a: A quick fix relieves symptoms but its side effects make the underlying problem worse over time.

the-cobra-effect-unintended-consequences.core: When you reward a metric, people optimise the metric, sometimes in ways that worsen the real goal (the cobra effect, Goodhart's law). Design incentives with loops in mind.

first_principles.problem: Paying per dead cobra led people to breed cobras. Rewarding 'tickets closed' or 'lines of code' produces trivial tickets and bloated code.
derivation: Ask: **how could this metric be gamed?**
Use **balanced sets** of metrics (speed + quality).
Reward **outcomes**, not proxies.
Review metrics for **side effects** after rollout.

analogy.title: The cobra bounty
analogy.story: Delhi paid for dead cobras; people bred cobras; when the bounty ended they released them, and there were more cobras than before.
analogy.breaks: The cobra story is extreme. Engineering gaming is usually subtle, so look for metric changes without outcome changes.

example.title: Rewarding low MTTR
example.scenario: Teams are rewarded for low mean time to resolve.

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: Pair MTTR with reopen rate and SLO impact.

example.outcome: metrics guide improvement instead of being gamed.

check.a: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.

finding-high-leverage-points.core: Not all interventions are equal. Tuning parameters (timeouts, thresholds) is low leverage; changing feedback loops, information flows, rules and goals is high leverage (Donella Meadows).

first_principles.problem: Engineers spend most effort tweaking numbers, which rarely changes system behaviour, while ignoring the structure, information and incentives that drive it.
truths: Goals and rules shape everything below.
derivation: **Low**: constants (buffer sizes, thresholds).
**Medium**: buffers, delays, feedback loop strength.
**High**: information flows (who sees what), rules (policies), goals.
**Highest**: paradigms (how people think about the system).

analogy.title: Steering a ship
analogy.story: Polishing the deck (parameters) does nothing for direction. Moving the rudder (rules, goals) changes where the whole ship goes.
analogy.breaks: A rudder works instantly. Changing organisational goals takes time and buy-in.

example.title: Cloud costs keep rising
flow: High: show each team its cost

steps.label: Information flow
steps.detail: Cost dashboards per team changed behaviour more than any manual resizing.

example.outcome: a small change in information produced a large change in outcomes.

check.q: Why is showing teams their own costs high leverage?
check.a: It changes the information driving their decisions, so they self-correct continuously.
